narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 59.8% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. You placed in the bottom decile (1 out of 10) of your class, far below the average of roughly the middle of the class among students who were accepted. This low ranking signaled to the model a higher risk that you would struggle with the bar exam.

Your LSAT score was the second most important factor and worked in your favor. At 38, your score sits slightly above the average of accepted students (37.18), which helped pull the prediction back toward passing.

Your family income bracket ranked third. Being from an upper-middle income family slightly increased the chance of failure according to the model, even though this group makes up 45% of accepted students.

Taken together, the very low third-year class rank outweighed the positive effect of your LSAT score and led the model to conclude you were more likely than not to fail the bar exam.

What you should do next is focus on improving your academic performance and class standing in the remaining part of your studies. Raising your grades and class rank will have the biggest impact on future predictions and on your actual likelihood of passing the bar. Consider seeking academic support or tutoring now to strengthen your trajectory.
